title: From Chained Books to Cheap Pages: How Printing Changed the World
title_zh: 从铁链锁住的书到廉价的书页：印刷术如何改变世界
intro_zh: 本文约 520 词，CET-4 难度，讲述印刷术如何改变世界：从锁在书架上的手抄本，到普通人买得起的印本，再到知识与日常生活的传播。

paragraphs.en: Before 1450, many European libraries fastened their books to the shelves with iron chains. This sounds strange today. The chains were not there to keep readers safe; they were there to protect the books, because a single handmade copy could cost as much as a small house. Almost nobody could own one.
paragraphs.zh: 1450 年以前，欧洲许多图书馆用铁链把书固定在书架上。这在今天听起来很奇怪。铁链不是为了保护读者，而是为了保护书，因为一本手抄本的价格可能相当于一幢小房子。几乎没有人能拥有一本书。

paragraphs.en: Making a book by hand was slow work. A skilled copyist working alone might need three years to finish one Bible. Every page was written with a pen made from a bird's feather, and every letter was shaped by hand. The work was careful, but the pace was painfully slow. A whole monastery might own only a handful of books.
paragraphs.zh: 手工制作一本书是件缓慢的活儿。一位熟练的抄写员独自工作，可能需要三年才能完成一本《圣经》。每一页都用羽毛笔写成，每一个字母都由手工描画。这项工作十分细致，但速度慢得令人痛苦。一整座修道院可能也只有寥寥几本书。

paragraphs.en: Then came Johannes Gutenberg, a goldsmith in Mainz, Germany. Around 1450 he found a new way to reproduce text. He cut each letter as a small metal block. Workers could arrange these blocks into a page, ink them, and press paper onto them. The metal letters could be used again and again, so one workshop could do the work of many copyists. In about two years his workshop produced roughly 180 copies of the Bible.
paragraphs.zh: 后来出现了约翰内斯·古腾堡，他是德国美因茨的一位金匠。大约在 1450 年，他找到了一种复制文字的新方法。他把每个字母刻成一个小金属块。工人们可以把这些金属块排成一页，涂上油墨，再把纸压上去。这些金属字母可以反复使用，因此一个作坊就能完成许多抄写员的工作。在大约两年时间里，他的作坊印制了约 180 本《圣经》。

paragraphs.en: The results were striking. Within fifty years, European workshops had printed an estimated twenty million books. Prices fell quickly, and a printed copy was far more affordable than a handwritten one. For the first time, ordinary families could buy a book of their own and keep it at home.
paragraphs.zh: 结果令人震惊。五十年内，欧洲各地的作坊估计印出了两千万册书。书价迅速下降，印本比手抄本便宜得多。普通家庭第一次能够买得起属于自己的书，并把它留在家中。

paragraphs.en: This changed who could read. For centuries, reading had been a skill of the church and the rich. Cheaper books created new readers, and new readers wanted even more books. In many towns, literacy slowly rose, and reading moved from a rare privilege to a normal part of daily life. Schools and shops began to use printed forms and notices.
paragraphs.zh: 这也改变了能读书的人。几个世纪以来，阅读一直是教会和富人的技能。更便宜的书造就了新的读者，而新读者又想要更多的书。在许多城镇，识字率慢慢上升，阅读从一种稀有的特权变成了日常生活的一部分。学校和店铺开始使用印刷的表格和告示。

paragraphs.en: Ideas began to circulate faster than ever before. In the early 1500s, short writings by Martin Luther reached thousands of towns in just a few weeks. Scientists could now compare the same page in different cities, so mistakes were easier to spot and correct. New maps and medical guides reached sailors and doctors quickly. Knowledge no longer stayed in one place.
paragraphs.zh: 思想开始以史无前例的速度传播。16 世纪初，马丁·路德的短文在短短几周内就传到了成千上万个城镇。科学家们如今可以比较不同城市的同一页内容，因此错误更容易被发现和纠正。新的地图和医学指南迅速传到水手和医生手中。知识不再停留在一个地方。

paragraphs.en: Everyday life changed too. Printers sold small pamphlets and news sheets for a few coins, and street sellers called out the latest stories. People read about storms, prices, and wars far from home. Ordinary families could own a songbook, a book of recipes, or a simple guide to farming. Printers even chose one spelling for a word, and millions of readers slowly copied it.
paragraphs.zh: 日常生活也发生了变化。印刷商以几个硬币的价格出售小册子和新闻纸，街头小贩叫卖最新的消息。人们读到远方发生的风暴、物价和战争。普通家庭可以拥有一本歌本、一本食谱或一本简单的农事指南。印刷商甚至为单词选定一种拼法，数百万读者慢慢照抄。

paragraphs.en: We should not pretend that the press only did good. Cheap printing spread false stories as well as true ones, and some governments tried hard to control what was printed. But the wider impact was clear. Information became accessible to far more people, and old ideas faced new questions.
paragraphs.zh: 我们不该假装印刷术只有好处。廉价的印刷既传播了假消息，也传播了真消息，一些政府还竭力控制印刷内容。但更广泛的影响是清楚的。信息变得更容易为更多人获取，旧观念也面临新的质疑。

paragraphs.en: Today we rarely think about the price of words. We copy a page with one touch and send it across the world. That small act would have seemed like magic in a room full of chained books. The printing press did not invent reading, but it made reading something ordinary people could share.
paragraphs.zh: 今天我们很少想到文字的价格。我们轻轻一触就能复制一页，并把它发送到世界各地。在那个满是锁链书籍的房间里，这个小小的动作简直像魔法。印刷术并没有发明阅读，但它让阅读成为普通人可以共享的事情。

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Handwritten books were more beautiful than printed ones.
The printing press made books cheap and helped knowledge spread widely.
Gutenberg was the first person in Europe to write a book.
Modern libraries still chain their books to the shelves.
questions.explain: 全文从铁链锁书的手抄本时代讲到印本价格下降、识字率上升、思想传播和日常生活变化，主旨是印刷术让书变便宜并推动知识广泛传播。A、C 与原文不符，D 是把历史现象误当作现状。

questions.q: According to the passage, how long might a skilled copyist need to finish one Bible?
questions.explain: 第二段明确说：一位熟练的抄写员可能需要三年（three years）才能抄完一本《圣经》。其余选项均为干扰项。

questions.q: Why does the writer mention the iron chains in the first paragraph?
options: To show that old libraries were dangerous for book thieves.
To show that Gutenberg invented iron chains.
To show how valuable and rare books once were.
To explain why today's libraries look different.
questions.explain: 铁链不是为了读者安全，而是因为一本手抄本贵得像一幢小房子，用来说明书曾经多么珍贵、稀少，从而衬托印刷术带来的变化。A、B 曲解原文，D 不是作者的写作目的。

questions.q: The word 'affordable' in paragraph 4 is closest in meaning to ___
options: easy to buy with the money you have
questions.explain: 第四段说同时代书价迅速下降，印本比手抄本 affordable，即价格低、人们买得起。故 affordable 意为‘买得起的、价格合理的’，选 A。
